How to Audit Your Daily Routine and Remove What Is Holding You Back

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:52
Instaread

There is plenty of good intent at the start of each working week. Few people turn up to work on Monday morning expecting to fill the week by stuffing themselves full of junk food, working late into the evening, not taking enough time for relaxation and then failing to clear all of the work that has been building up during the week. By Wednesday afternoon most people are exhausted and are plodding along on auto pilot. Most work is reacted to rather than managed. Such work leads to tired eyes and a worn out feeling at the end of the long working day.

Chances are you are losing a ton of energy just trying to manage your daily habits and dealing with physical friction. But your daily routine is full of these often hidden habits, which when taken out one by one can greatly improve your energy levels. Doing an audit of your daily routine is a powerful way to understand what you’re getting out of your current habits and then remove things that aren’t useful to you.

Tidying Up Your Workspace and Protecting Your Senses

A thorough daily audit begins with the immediate physical environment where you spend the bulk of your working hours. If you work at a computer, your desk setup plays a massive part in your overall stamina. Slumping over a laptop on a low dining room table or working in poor room lighting creates an immediate drain on your focus.

One area that frequently gets neglected is daily eye health. Staring at backlit monitors for eight or nine hours straight causes digital fatigue, dry eyes, and late-afternoon tension headaches. Taking simple steps like adjusting your screen height to eye level, following the 20-20-20 rule, and wearing lightweight round glasses fitted with anti-glare lenses can make desk work significantly more comfortable. Beyond the practical visual clarity, comfortable eyewear that suits your face shape can give you an extra boost of confidence when jumping on video calls or working in busy shared offices. When you remove small physical discomforts from your workspace, staying focused throughout the day requires far less conscious effort.

Rebuilding the Foundations of Mind and Body

You can’t build sustained productivity on top of a tired body. When auditing your daily routine, start with your physical health and the type of fuel you’re using to power your body.

People reach for quick sugar for a energy boost in the short term but after a blood sugar crash they are left feeling tired, grumpy and unable to concentrate. A good diet consists of whole foods that contain complex carbohydrates, proteins and plenty of water. This provides steady energy and means you are no longer relying on your body’s supply of adrenaline to get you through to the end of the day.

In the same way, demarcating your time for work and your time for personal life and activities will also affect your mental well-being. As mentioned earlier, starting the day by scrolling through work e-mails in your bed has a negative effect on you within seconds. Creating habits such as leaving the house within ten minutes or reading a chapter before you start checking your phone can set you up for a wonderful start to the day and get you off to a calm and intentional start.

Structuring a Systematic Routine That Actually Sticks

One of the biggest mistakes that people try to change too many things at once. While it may be tempting to download 10 new productivity apps to your phone and try to stick to a strict new schedule, chances are within a week you’ll have burned yourself out and be back to normal.

By allowing yourself to operate according to your natural rhythms you are able to develop a systematic and organized routine that allows you to work to your full potential.

  • Determine your most productive prime focus hours: Identify when you are most focused during the day. Typically, it is early in the morning and lasts for 2-3 hours (i.e. 9 AM-11 AM). Protect these hours from routine activities, i.e. schedule and deal with administrative items in the late afternoon when your energy has come back.
  • Batching similar tasks together: These days many people are switching between different tasks like reading emails, writing reports and monitoring social media platforms all day long. This type of context switching leads to big losses of energy and can cause a feeling of being worn out. Working in batches of similar tasks helps to maximize productivity while preserving mental energy.
  • Mandatory micro-breaks in your workday: Taking five minutes every hour to stretch and walk to the water-cooler to refuel, recharges your batteries throughout the day.
  • End the day as systematically as you begin it – by shutting down. The end of your working day needs to be a clear and complete end to your work.
  • Take 15 minutes to clear your workspace, to write down three tasks to be dealt with the next working day, to shut down all applications on your computer and close all your browser windows.

Practical Daily Audit Framework

To make your routine audit easier to manage, look at your day across these key checkpoints:

Audit Category

Common Daily Obstacle

Practical Adjustment

Workspace and Vision

Staring at harsh screens with poor posture

Adjust monitor height, use anti-reflective lenses, and take regular screen breaks

Nutrition and Energy

Midday energy crashes from sugary snacks

Drink plenty of water and build meals around whole foods and lean proteins

Movement and Body

Sitting motionless in an office chair for hours

Take short standing breaks, stretch your hips, and add a brisk daily walk

Mental Boundaries

Checking work emails late at night in bed

Turn off work notifications after hours and create a dedicated evening wind-down

Removing the Friction Gradually

Life is unpredictable and much can happen from one day to the next. The daily routine audit is not intended to form the basis of a person’s future striving for perfection. Rather, it reveals to us, which routines are negative for our energy and, what can be done to change this. It is not about becoming a machine but about forming healthy routines that support us in our goals.

Begin with a single change to your current routine. Set aside time to organize your space, identify what time of day you will check your emails or set a “stop work” time for the day. Slowly but surely begin to identify and cut out all of the things that are sucking the life out of you. It won’t be long before you’ve established a truly sustainable and healthy routine for daily living.
